notes:
Below are my notes on 1 John 3. I couldn't get to several of the sources you named, including Enduring Word and the full verse-by-verse pages on Bible Hub and StudyLight. That leaves the notes uneven. Verse 9 is covered in depth, verses 1–8 and 13–18 are partly covered, and **I found nothing on verses 11–12 or 19–24**, so I've left those out. The gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Part 1: Traditional reading

**v. 1:** Augustine says believers are both *called* and actually *are* God's sons. He also says there is a godly "world" and an ungodly "world" spread through all nations, and the ungodly one does not know the godly. Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called, and should be, the sons of God... There is a whole world Christian, and a whole world ungodly https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170204.htm
- The Bridgeway commentary (Fleming) says God's children now think and act like their heavenly Father. Unbelievers, who go by the world's standards, can't understand them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Chuck Smith (Smith's Bible Commentary) treats the verse as wonder that God would adopt and claim us as His sons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 2:** Fleming says believers know little about the life to come, but they do know they will in some way be like Christ. That is a reason to become as much like Him as possible now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Smith says Scripture doesn't describe heaven in detail because no human words could. He adds that the Spirit is changing believers into Christ's image day by day, so Christ's appearing should not be a sudden reversal of how they live. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 3:** Augustine says "even as He is pure" means likeness, not equality: He is pure from eternity, we pure by faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170204.htm
- Fleming: believers should be pure in thought and behaviour, as Christ was. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 4:** Augustine warns against anyone saying they are a sinner but not "a doer of iniquity." For John, sin *is* iniquity. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170204.htm
- Fleming sees John answering false teachers who said knowledge was all that mattered and behaviour didn't. Against them, John defines sin as breaking God's law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**vv. 5–6:** Fleming: people who deliberately keep on sinning know neither God, who gave the law, nor Christ, who takes away sin. John isn't saying Christians can't sin (1:6–10 rules that out), but that they don't sin as they please or as a habit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Spurgeon on "whoever abides in Him sins not": it can't mean a believer never sins. It means that sins not habitually, he sins not designedly, he sins not finally, so as to perish. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 7:** Augustine again says "as He is righteous" means resemblance, not equality. Even when our righteousness is made perfect it will never equal God's. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170204.htm

**v. 8:** Wesley concludes that the "works of the devil" Christ came to destroy are sin, and the fruits of sin. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-62-the-end-of-christs-coming/
- Augustine: you become a child of the devil by imitating him, not because he created or fathered you. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170204.htm
- Fleming: a person's behaviour shows whether they belong to Christ or to the devil, and no one can belong to both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 9:** The usual evangelical reading takes the present-tense verbs to mean ongoing, habitual sin. Precept Austin quotes John Stott: John is arguing rather the incongruity than the impossibility of sin in the Christian. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_39_commentary
- Gill: the believer doesn't make sin his trade and business. He still has sin in him and commits sinful acts, but he isn't its slave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- GotQuestions: since 1:8 calls anyone who claims to have no sin a liar, 3:9 can't mean sinlessness. It means that whoever is born of God will no longer continue to sin willfully or habitually. https://www.gotquestions.org/does-not-sin.html
- **What the "seed" is.** Barnes notes the options: God's word (the view of Augustine, Clement and others) or God's Spirit. His own view is that it is the "germ of piety" planted by the word and Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Bible Hub's Q&A page reads the seed as the Holy Spirit living in the believer. https://biblehub.com/q/does_1_john_3_9_say_christians_never_sin.htm

**v. 10:** Wesley: by this "plain mark," committing sin or not, God's children and the devil's children are told apart. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-18-the-marks-of-the-new-birth/
- Fleming: true Christians have a divine power inside them fighting the devil. Habitual sin shows a person is not a Christian. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**v. 13:** Augustine: "the world" that hates us means people who love the world, not heaven, earth or God's creation. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170205.htm

**vv. 14–15:** Augustine warns that no one should treat hatred, or simply failing to love, as a small thing, because John calls the hater a murderer. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170205.htm

**vv. 16–17:** Augustine: if you aren't yet ready to die for your brother, at least be ready to give him your goods. For if your superfluities you can not give to your brother, can you lay down your life for your brother? https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170205.htm

**v. 18:** Augustine: giving should come from real mercy, not from wanting to be admired. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170205.htm

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ (mainly v. 9, also vv. 6 and 8)

**Methodist and Wesleyan (John Wesley, Adam Clarke)**
- Wesley rejects the "habitual" reading outright. Of those who add "habitually," he says: Whence is that I read it not. It is not written in the Book. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-18-the-marks-of-the-new-birth/
- In Sermon 19 he defines the sin in view as outward, voluntary breaking of a known command of God. While a believer stays in faith, love and prayer, he not only doth not, but cannot, thus commit sin. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-19-the-great-privilege-of-those-that-are-born-of-god/
- He admits that people truly born of God, such as David and Peter, did sin. His explanation is that this happens only when they stop "keeping" themselves. Inward sin comes first and faith is lost before outward sin follows. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/sermons.v.xix.html
- In *A Plain Account of Christian Perfection* he uses v. 8 to argue that Christ destroys the devil's works "without any limitation." He concludes that A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/a-plain-account-of-christian-perfection/
- Adam Clarke also says the "habitual" reading brings the new birth's privileges very low indeed. He argues that even pagan philosophers mastered their vices. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**Reformed (Calvin, Barnes)**
- Calvin: regeneration isn't complete in this life, so God's children still sin every day. Even so, the Spirit restrains sin so it can't rule them. He reads "cannot sin" as the Spirit keeping the elect in obedience so effectively that "inflexible perseverance" is joined to new life.
- Calvin argues against Catholic theologians who taught that the Spirit leaves us free to choose good or evil. Discussing David, he says the incorruptible seed can be smothered, but a "live coal" stays hidden under the ashes. He also notes that John means the ongoing course of life, not single acts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Barnes: the verse means either habitual sin or absolute perfection, and no one can seriously hold the second. He concludes that no words could more clearly prove that true Christians will never fall from grace (his sentence is about one who is renewed never again becoming characteristically a sinner). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

**Charismatic Reformed (Sam Storms)**
- Storms weighs several views. He rejects the "old nature sins, new nature can't" view because it is always the *person* who sins. He sides with most commentators: the sin meant is habitual, persistent and unrepentant.
- On grammar, he notes "to sin" is a present infinitive. If it were aorist, John would be contradicting 2:1. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/1-john-3:9-and-the-doctrine-of-perseverance

**Baptist and Dispensational (Gill, Deffinbaugh)**
- Gill reads the verse as habitual sin. He also suggests that the new nature itself, being pure and holy, cannot sin. Storms rejects exactly this view. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/1-john/3-9.html
- Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org) links the verse to eternal security: If a person could sin and loses their salvation, how can it be said that God's seed remains in that person? https://bible.org/seriespage/q-does-1-john-39-teach-christians-must-be-sinless

**Churches of Christ (Coffman)**
- Coffman says "cannot sin" states what is *forbidden*, not what is impossible. His illustration is "you cannot turn right on red." He identifies the seed as the word of God.
- He says free will can fail, so a believer can still sin. He lists views he considers wrong, including the "old nature did it" view and the "mortal sins only" view that he attributes to Catholics. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship (v. 9)**
- The NET Bible note says the verse draws a sharp contrast: the one who practises sin is of the devil (v. 8), the one fathered by God does not. It points to S. Kubo's study, which reads John's argument as a contrast between true Christians and the heretics opposing them. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1Jo&chapter=3&verse=9
- Constable, citing Marshall and Dodd, says the Greek present tense doesn't always mean habitual action. It often describes absolute action. He also notes that the NET translation itself handles 3:6 and 3:9 inconsistently. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- A Precept Austin page lists a weakness of the habitual view: it depends on a grammatical subtlety which an interpreter cannot stress in other places in the New Testament. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59497/

**Catholic (Augustine via New Advent)**
- Augustine sets out the believer's dilemma. If he admits he is a sinner, he fears he is "not born of God." If he claims to be sinless, 1:8 condemns him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/170205.htm
- I didn't reach the part of Homily 5 where he resolves this, so I can't report his answer. As noted above, Coffman claims Catholic writers limit the verse to "mortal" sins. That is his description, not a Catholic source.

**Using the verse as a licence to sin**
- Calvin condemns people who say that since believers "cannot sin," everything is permitted to them, adultery and theft included. He answers that believers don't sin because God has written His law on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- Coffman lists a similar error: the idea that what is sinful for unbelievers isn't sinful for Christians. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/3-9.html
- These are historical warnings. I found nothing on modern hyper-grace, prosperity or word-of-faith readings of this chapter. That includes "whatever we ask" in v. 22.

---

**What I couldn't find:** Enduring Word; Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary; any Lutheran (LCMS, 1517) or Pentecostal (AG, Pneuma Review) source; Orthodox (OCA) material; and any note at all on verses 11–12 and 19–24. Augustine's Homily 6 on New Advent covers 3:19–4:3, but I didn't read it. Those are the next things to check.
